title: Fever and cough in a 42-year-old man
opening_brief:
You are a medical student in the general medicine outpatient clinic.

A 42-year-old man has come in with fever and cough for the last three days.

Your objective is to take a history, examine him, select appropriate investigations, build a differential diagnosis and explain your reasoning.

patient.name: Suresh Nair
patient.background: Lives with his wife and two children. Has not seen a doctor in years.

persona.speech_style: Plain, slightly breathless, gives short answers.
persona.emotional_state: Uncomfortable and tired, wants to feel better quickly.
knows_not: the names of any medicines beyond 'a fever tablet'
what his blood pressure usually is
quirks: Coughs mid-sentence when talking for too long.

chief_complaint: fever with cough for three days

present_illness.onset: Started three days ago, quite suddenly, with a shaking chill.
present_illness.site: Chest pain on the right side, low down, near the ribs.
present_illness.character: The chest pain is sharp, like a catch.
present_illness.severity: Fever feels high; pain 6 out of 10 when it comes.
present_illness.timing: Fever is worse in the evening. Cough is all day.
present_illness.aggravating: Deep breathing and coughing make the chest pain much worse.
present_illness.relieving: Lying still on the painful side helps a little. A fever tablet helped briefly.
associated: cough bringing up thick rusty-brown phlegm
feeling short of breath when walking to the toilet
present_illness.progression: Getting worse each day, especially the breathlessness.

past_medical: No diabetes or blood pressure that he knows of
Had jaundice as a teenager, recovered fully
medications: Only a paracetamol tablet bought from the pharmacy
family: Father died of a heart attack at 60
social: Smokes about 10 bidis a day for 20 years
No known contact with anyone coughing for a long time
review_of_systems_positive: chest hurts when breathing in deeply

examination.label: Vital signs
examination.result: Temperature 39.1 C. Pulse 108/min regular. BP 118/74 mmHg. Respiratory rate 26/min. SpO2 92% on room air.

examination.label: General examination
examination.result: Unwell, flushed, breathing shallowly. No pallor, no cyanosis, no clubbing, no icterus. No palpable lymph nodes. Mildly dehydrated.

examination.label: Full respiratory examination
examination.result: Inspection: reduced movement of the right lower chest, no scars or deformity. Percussion: dull over the right lower zone posteriorly, resonant elsewhere. Auscultation: bronchial breath sounds with coarse end-inspiratory crackles over the right lower zone, with increased vocal resonance in the same area. Left lung clear.

examination.label: Respiratory inspection and expansion
examination.result: Reduced movement of the right lower chest. No scars or deformity.

examination.label: Chest percussion
examination.result: Dull to percussion over the right lower zone posteriorly. Resonant elsewhere.

examination.label: Chest auscultation
examination.result: Bronchial breath sounds with coarse end-inspiratory crackles over the right lower zone. Increased vocal resonance in the same area. Left lung clear.

examination.label: Cardiovascular examination
examination.result: Heart sounds normal, no murmur. JVP not raised. No pedal oedema.

examination.label: Abdominal examination
examination.result: Soft, non-tender. Liver and spleen not enlarged.

examination.label: Lower limb examination
examination.result: Both calves equal in circumference, non-tender. No pedal oedema, no erythema, no palpable cord.

examination.label: Chest wall palpation
examination.result: No tenderness on palpation of the chest wall or costochondral junctions. The pain is not reproduced by pressing; it is reproduced by deep inspiration.

investigations.label: Chest X-ray (PA)
investigations.result: Homogeneous opacity involving the right lower lobe with air bronchograms. No pleural effusion. Heart size normal.

investigations.label: Complete blood count
investigations.result: Hb 13.4 g/dL. Total WBC 18,600/uL with 86% neutrophils. Platelets 265,000/uL.

investigations.label: Sputum Gram stain and culture
investigations.result: Gram stain: numerous polymorphs with Gram-positive diplococci. Culture pending at 48 hours.

investigations.label: Sputum for AFB / GeneXpert
investigations.result: No acid-fast bacilli seen on two samples. GeneXpert: MTB not detected.

investigations.label: Renal function and electrolytes
investigations.result: Urea 38 mg/dL. Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. Na 134 mEq/L. K 4.1 mEq/L.

investigations.label: Arterial blood gas
investigations.result: pH 7.46, PaO2 62 mmHg, PaCO2 32 mmHg, HCO3 23 on room air.

investigations.label: Blood culture
investigations.result: Sent before antibiotics. No growth at 24 hours; final result pending.

investigations.label: CT chest
investigations.result: Right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms. No mass, no cavitation, no effusion.
investigations.note: Adds nothing over the chest X-ray in a straightforward community-acquired pneumonia.

investigations.label: Dengue NS1 and serology
investigations.note: Reasonable in an undifferentiated fever, low yield once focal chest signs are present.

investigations.label: D-dimer
investigations.note: Raised, and uninterpretable here. D-dimer rises in any inflammatory or infective state, so a positive result in established pneumonia does not raise the probability of pulmonary embolism — it only generates a CT. Use clinical probability first.

differentials.why: Abrupt fever with rigor, rusty sputum, focal consolidation signs, neutrophilic leucocytosis and lobar opacity on X-ray.
Endemic and must be excluded in any Indian patient with fever and cough, but the three-day onset, rigor and lobar consolidation argue against it. Excluded here on AFB and GeneXpert.
Pleuritic pain with hypoxia and tachycardia can be embolic; the fever, purulent sputum and consolidation make it unlikely, but it should be consciously considered.
Common cause of fever and cough, but does not produce focal dullness, bronchial breathing or lobar opacity.
Can follow pneumonia; no cavitation or foul sputum at this stage.
Viral pneumonitis is usually bilateral and interstitial rather than lobar with rusty sputum.
No orthopnoea, raised JVP, oedema or cardiomegaly.

final_diagnosis: Community-acquired pneumonia of the right lower lobe, most likely pneumococcal, with hypoxia (CURB-65 = 1, but SpO2 92% warrants admission)
diagnosis_reasoning: Abrupt onset fever with a rigor, pleuritic right-sided chest pain, rusty sputum, focal dullness with bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance, neutrophilic leucocytosis and a lobar opacity with air bronchograms together make lobar pneumonia the only diagnosis that explains every finding. Gram-positive diplococci on sputum support Streptococcus pneumoniae.

history.label: Onset and duration of the fever
history.teaching_note: Abrupt onset with a rigor separates bacterial pneumonia from the indolent onset of tuberculosis.

history.label: Character of the sputum
history.teaching_note: Rusty sputum is close to pathognomonic for pneumococcal pneumonia. Missing it means missing the single most specific clue in the history.

history.label: Blood in the sputum
history.teaching_note: Separates pneumonia from TB, bronchiectasis and malignancy.

history.label: Chest pain and its relation to breathing
history.teaching_note: Pleuritic pain localises the pathology to the pleura and narrows the differential immediately.

history.label: Breathlessness and exercise tolerance
history.teaching_note: Quantifying breathlessness drives the severity assessment and the decision to admit.

history.label: Weight loss and night sweats
history.teaching_note: Constitutional symptoms are the screening question for tuberculosis, which is the must-exclude diagnosis here.

history.label: Contact with a person with tuberculosis
history.teaching_note: In a TB-endemic setting, contact history is not optional.

history.label: Smoking history
history.teaching_note: Smoking predisposes to pneumococcal disease and to malignancy, and changes the differential for a persistent opacity.

history.label: Alcohol use
history.teaching_note: Alcohol excess predisposes to aspiration and to Klebsiella pneumonia.

history.label: Diabetes, HIV or other comorbidity
history.teaching_note: Immunosuppression changes both the likely organism and the disposition.

history.label: Recent travel or exposure
history.teaching_note: Relevant to atypical organisms and to endemic infections.

history.label: Medication already taken
history.teaching_note: Prior antibiotics change culture yield and the fever pattern.

examination.label: Vital signs including oxygen saturation
examination.teaching_note: SpO2 92% and a respiratory rate of 26 are what move this patient from outpatient to inpatient care.

examination.label: Full respiratory examination
examination.teaching_note: Dullness with bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance is the classic triad of consolidation.

examination.label: Cardiovascular examination
examination.teaching_note: Excludes heart failure as a cause of the breathlessness.

examination.label: General examination
examination.teaching_note: Clubbing and lymphadenopathy would point away from simple pneumonia.

examination.label: Lower limbs for DVT
examination.teaching_note: Pleuritic pain with hypoxia can be embolic. Examining the calves is how you consciously address pulmonary embolism rather than assuming pneumonia because there is a fever.

examination.label: Chest wall palpation
examination.teaching_note: Distinguishes pleuritic pain from a musculoskeletal cause. Pain reproduced by pressing points away from the pleura.

investigations.label: Chest X-ray
investigations.teaching_note: The single test that confirms consolidation and defines its extent.

investigations.label: Complete blood count
investigations.teaching_note: Neutrophilic leucocytosis supports a bacterial cause.

investigations.label: Sputum for AFB / GeneXpert
investigations.teaching_note: In India, TB must be actively excluded before labelling a chest opacity as pneumonia.

investigations.label: Renal function and electrolytes
investigations.teaching_note: Urea is a component of CURB-65 and drives the admission decision.

investigations.label: Blood culture
investigations.teaching_note: Low yield but changes management when positive; must be taken before antibiotics.

hints: Look again at the vital signs and at where in the chest the abnormal findings are.
The examination findings are all confined to one lobe. What single process produces dullness, bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance together?
Review the causes of an acute febrile illness with focal signs confined to one part of the chest, and how you would separate them from tuberculosis.
teaching_points: Dullness + bronchial breath sounds + increased vocal resonance = consolidation, and consolidation with acute fever means pneumonia until proven otherwise.
Use CURB-65 (confusion, urea >42 mg/dL, respiratory rate >=30, BP <90/60, age >=65) to decide disposition, but treat hypoxia as an independent reason to admit.
In a TB-endemic setting, always send sputum for AFB/GeneXpert even when the clinical picture looks bacterial.
Rusty sputum, a preceding rigor and lobar consolidation together point to Streptococcus pneumoniae.
